Why We Started Barrel

When we first started Barrel, we were building a tool to help businesses manage procurement. The idea was to make it easier for teams to create their own workflows for purchase requests, approvals, and other processes without needing to build custom software.

But as people started using the product, we noticed something interesting.

Some of our users weren't just building procurement workflows. They were finding ways to use Barrel for other internal processes we hadn't originally designed it for.

That caught our attention. We had built the product around a particular problem, but customers seemed to be telling us there was something bigger worth exploring.

So we started talking to them.

Over the course of hundreds of interviews, we spent time understanding how businesses managed their day-to-day operations, particularly across HR, IT, and finance.

One thing kept coming up: companies already had plenty of software, but their teams were still doing a surprising amount of work manually.

An employee joining a company, for example, could trigger several tasks across different systems. Someone needed to update employee records, arrange equipment, provision software access, and follow up on approvals. Even though the company had tools for all these things, someone still had to coordinate everything.

The more we learned, the more we questioned whether building another workflow tool was really the answer.

What if, instead of giving people software to manage their work, we could build software that actually did more of the work for them?

That question changed the direction of Barrel.

What We Built

We moved beyond procurement and started building Enterprise AI Agents.

The idea was to let employees describe what they needed in plain English and have AI agents help execute the necessary workflows across their existing systems.

We focused on three areas: people, money, and technology operations.

That included things like managing employee information, coordinating software and device access, and handling internal spending requests and approvals.

Rather than expecting employees to navigate multiple applications to complete a task, we wanted Barrel to help coordinate the process from one place.

My Role

As Founder and CEO, I led the product direction, from understanding what customers needed to deciding what we should build.

The biggest decision was moving away from our original procurement-focused product. We had already invested time in building it, so changing direction wasn't something I took lightly.

But the feedback we were getting made it difficult to ignore the broader problem.

I worked closely with customers to understand their workflows, translate those needs into product requirements, and prioritize what belonged in our first version.

One challenge was deciding how much an AI agent should actually do. Some tasks could be automated, while others needed approvals or human involvement. We had to think beyond whether the technology could perform an action to whether a business would trust it to do so.

We also had to keep the product focused. HR, IT, and finance cover a lot of ground, and trying to solve everything at once wasn't realistic.

Results & Learnings

We built the first version of Barrel and worked with enterprise design partners to test how AI agents could support their internal workflows.

The experience taught me a lot about building enterprise products, particularly how different what customers initially ask for can be from the problem they're actually trying to solve.

It also changed how I think about product discovery.

If we had focused only on making our procurement workflow builder better, we might never have noticed what customers were trying to accomplish with it outside procurement.

Barrel eventually shut down, but building it remains one of my most important product experiences.

I learned how to question an initial product thesis, make difficult prioritization decisions, work through the challenges of building AI-powered workflows, and take a product from an idea into customers' hands.

More than anything, Barrel taught me to pay attention to what people actually do with a product, not just what you originally built it for.
